body_markdown:
An Expert Interview with Joseph Costello, Clinical Director at Miracles Asia, the Top Holistic Addiction Treatment Centre in Thailand, Combining CBT, EMDR, 12-Step and Mindfulness to Treat Mind, Body and Spirit


****


At Gainful, we believe that real, lasting progress in fitness and nutrition comes from consistency over time, not from perfect days or peak motivation. We build personalized performance nutrition because we know that sustainable results depend on routines that actually hold up in the real world. Today, we're sitting down with Joseph Costello, Clinical Director at Miracles Asia, the top holistic addiction treatment centre in Thailand. Joseph works every day with people navigating some of the most demanding behavioral change processes imaginable. His clinical perspective on habit formation, sustainable routines, and the psychology of long-term progress applies directly to anyone pursuing meaningful change in their health, fitness, or performance.


****


Q: Joseph, your clinical work at Miracles Asia centers on sustainable behavioral change in a recovery context. What is the most important thing people misunderstand about what actually drives lasting change?


****


A:


The biggest misconception is that motivation is the engine. People wait to feel ready, wait to feel inspired, or assume that if they were just disciplined enough they would follow through. But motivation is a feeling, and feelings are unreliable. What actually drives lasting change is structure. When the right behaviors are built into your environment, your schedule, and your daily sequence of decisions, you don't have to rely on how you feel that morning to determine whether you show up. In addiction recovery, we see this clearly. The people who sustain long-term sobriety are not the ones who wanted it most intensely in their first week. They are the ones who built a system of habits, accountability, and environmental cues that made the healthy choice the default choice, even on the days motivation was nowhere to be found.


****


Q: How should someone approach goal-setting if the goal is not short-term performance but genuine, long-term behavior change?


****


A:


Start smaller than feels meaningful, and be more specific than feels necessary. Vague goals like "get healthier" or "be more consistent" give you no behavioral target to aim at and no way to measure progress. Specific, realistic goals give your nervous system something to orient toward. In clinical practice, we use structured goal-setting frameworks that break a large outcome into the smallest repeatable actions that produce it. For someone building a fitness or nutrition routine, that might mean deciding exactly when, where, and how a habit will occur before the day begins, rather than leaving it to willpower in the moment. The goal is not to be ambitious. The goal is to be specific enough that success is achievable on an ordinary day, not just a great one.


****


Q: What role do environmental cues and routine architecture play in helping people stay consistent, and how can someone design their environment to support their goals?


****


A:


Environment is one of the most underused tools in behavior change, and one of the most powerful. The research is clear: behavior is heavily shaped by context. If the cues in your environment point toward the habits you want to build, consistency becomes easier. If they point away from those habits, willpower alone rarely compensates. In recovery, we work explicitly on restructuring the environments and routines that were associated with destructive patterns, because the environment itself is a trigger. For someone pursuing fitness or nutrition goals, the same principle applies in a practical, positive direction. Preparing your gym bag the night before, having your Gainful protein ready to go, eating at consistent times, removing friction from the behaviors you want to repeat: these are not tricks. They are the architecture of a functional habit system.


****


Q: Setbacks are inevitable in any long-term behavior change effort. How should people think about and respond to them without losing ground?


****


A:


The response to a setback matters far more than the setback itself. In clinical work, we pay close attention to what happens in the hours and days after a lapse, because that is often where the real damage is done, not in the lapse itself but in the shame spiral and all-or-nothing thinking that follows it. "I missed a day, so the week is ruined." "I went off my nutrition plan once, so I've failed." These narratives are not accurate, but they feel true in the moment, and they cause people to abandon systems that were otherwise working. The more effective framework is to treat a setback as data rather than evidence of personal failure. What happened? What was the trigger? What can be adjusted? One missed workout or one difficult meal does not erase consistent effort. The goal is not perfection. It is the ability to return to your system quickly and without self-punishment.


****


Q: For someone just beginning to build a sustainable routine around fitness, nutrition, or recovery, what is your single most important piece of advice?


****


A:


Decide in advance what you will do when it gets hard, because it will get hard. Most people design their routines for their best days and then have no plan for their average ones. In behavioral health, we call this an implementation intention: a specific, pre-committed response to a predictable obstacle. "If I miss a morning workout, I will do fifteen minutes in the evening instead of skipping entirely." "If I travel and can't follow my usual nutrition routine, I will prioritize protein and not treat the whole day as a loss." Having that plan in place before the difficulty arrives keeps you inside the system rather than outside it. Consistency, over months and years, is what produces results in fitness, in nutrition, in recovery, and in any domain where real change is the goal. The system is what makes consistency possible when motivation alone would not be enough.
